title: Warp-banked KV streaming and launch coalescing notes
content:
Summary:

This note collects notes and microbench results from exploring a warp-banked approach for streaming paged KV entries into inference kernels and a coarse launch-coalescing heuristic to amortize CUDA launch overhead for tiny requests. The goal: reduce end-to-end token latency tail for low-concurrency workloads (PLG warm-starts) while preserving throughput for high-concurrency bursts.

Motivation / problem statement:
- In hosted inference we often see a bimodal distribution: many requests produce very short decode steps (1-8 tokens) and a minority produce long sequences.
- Per-token kernel launch + small memcpy overhead dominates latency for short sequences, especially when KV pages are cold or sharded across device memory regions.
- Existing prefetch strategies pull whole pages synchronously or rely on global prefetch queues; that either increases memory pressure or adds latency spikes.

Hypothesis: warp-banked streaming + double-buffering + launch coalescing will reduce tail latency by:
1) overlapping async device page stage with compute using a dedicated set of CUDA streams (one stream per warp-bank).
2) compressing KV on the fly (lightweight 4-bit -> 16-bit expansions in-register) to reduce memory footprint and DMA time.
3) grouping tiny token-advance launches into a single kernel when they target contiguous or same page KV ranges (coalescer in runtime scheduler).

Design sketch:
- Warp-banked streamer: split the block grid into B 'warp-banks'. Each warp-bank owns a CUDA stream and a small ring-buffer region in device memory (page staging area). Kernels that will consume KV page X check a per-page owner hint; if owner != current warp-bank then runtime issues async copy to that bank's staging region on its dedicated stream.

- Double-buffered consumption: consumer kernel reads from staging buffer A while page streamer may be copying into B. Switch pointers via atomic flag and small handshake (cudaEvent / atomic int). This keeps consumer kernels lightweight (no per-element conditionals).

- Launch coalescer: runtime inspects microbatch queue (requests in same millisecond) and coalesces up to N tiny launches into one composite kernel when their KV page sets are disjoint OR fully overlap (fast-path). If they overlap partially, we fallback to separate launches to avoid complex synchronizations. Coalescing is best-effort and disabled if a request is latency-sensitive (explicit flag).

Kernel interface (recommended):
- __global__ void consume_kv_warpbank(float* staging_ptrs[], int page_meta[], int page_count, ConsumerArgs args)
  - staging_ptrs: array of B pointers (one per warp-bank), small and passed as kernel parameter.
  - page_meta: compact metadata per page (page_id, quant_format, length, block_stride).
  - ConsumerArgs: fused params (attention mask, seq_len, writeback pointer). Keep this small.

Implementation notes / CUDA specifics:
- Use cudaMemcpyAsync + cudaMemPrefetchAsync where supported (managed pinned) to move pages into device staging. Prefer pinned host -> device if host side fetch is required.
- Assign one persistent cudaStream_t per warp-bank to avoid stream creation overhead. Reuse streams across requests.
- Use cudaEventRecord to handshake buffer switches. Avoid blocking cudaStreamSynchronize inside hot path.
- For on-the-fly dequant: implement a tiny warp-level expansion that reads 4-bit packed values and writes FP16 into staging area using __shfl_sync based unpacking for coalesced reads. This keeps the DMA payload small and moves the decompression cost to the GPU where cycles are cheap compared to PCIe.
- For NVLink/peer copies in multi-gpu private deployments, consider cudaMemcpyPeerAsync into the same warp-bank staging region (performant vs remote page mapping).

Microbench experiments (summary):
- Setup: A100-40GB, single model layer (1 head, hidden 4096), synthetic inputs mimicking length=1 tokens at 100 qps. Baseline: naive per-token kernel launch + synchronous page copy.
- Results (median / p95 latency for a single-token advance):
  - Baseline (sync copy + launch): median 6.2ms, p95 18.9ms
  - Double-buffered warp-banked streamer (no coalesce): median 3.9ms, p95 8.7ms
  - Streamer + light-weight 4->16-bit expand in-flight: median 3.5ms, p95 7.8ms
  - Streamer + launch-coalescer (coalesce window 2-4 requests): median 2.6ms, p95 4.9ms
- Observations: the biggest wins are from avoiding synchronous host-device stalls and amortizing launch overhead when coalescing 2-4 tiny requests. Dequant on-device gave modest wins for PCIe-bound tests (~10-12% latency improvement) but is neutral on NVLink setups.

Heuristics for runtime integration:
- Coalescing policy: enable when (avg_seq_len <= 4) AND (concurrency < 16) AND (coalesce_window_ms <= 5). We measured diminishing returns beyond 4 requests.
- Page-owner heuristics: prefer affinity mapping based on last-consumer GPU stream to minimize cross-bank copies. If a page is hot (access count > threshold) pin it to its owning warp-bank for T seconds.
- Fall-back: if coalesced kernel would exceed shared-memory or register budgets, fall back to individual launches. Report telemetry for any fallback.

Telemetry to add (low cost):
- per-request: coalesced_flag (true/false), coalesced_group_size (int), page_copy_ms, kernel_launch_ms, total_token_advance_ms
- per-page: last_access_ts, owner_bank, hotness_score, size_bytes, quant_format
- kernel-level counters: buffer_switch_count, stream_waits, dequant_cycles_est (approx)

Edge cases and caveats:
- Partial overlap across pages: coalescing must ensure writeback lanes don't conflict. This requires a cheap intersection test at coalesce time; avoid doing expensive set-unions.
- Multi-tenant GPUs: warp-bank dedicated streams assume some fairness; in heavy noisy co-tenancy this can starve other work. Mitigate by making B configurable and auto-reducing when scheduler detects host contention.
- Kernel complexity: fused kernels that also do FlashAttention may increase register pressure. If register usage grows beyond occupancy sweet spot, throughput can regress; implement a build-time autotuner that emits two kernel variants (low-reg and high-reg) and pick at runtime via occupancy model.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Try microbench with T4 and V100 to see behavior with older PCIe stacks. Early small runs suggest more benefit on PCIe machines.
- Evaluate effect on token-quality: ensure that coalescing doesn't change scheduling/timing for timeout-sensitive callbacks or streaming responses.
- Experiment with adaptive coalescing window that uses moving-average of arrival gaps rather than fixed ms window.

Next steps / action items:
- Prototype consumer kernel with staging pointer array and double-buffer handshake (owner: Ethan). Target PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serve/pull/4823 (WIP).
- Add coalescer to runtime request queue as opt-in flag behind feature gate (Liam to add config + telemetry).
- Add small microbench harness to measure page copy vs on-device dequant (Sofia). Collect results for T4/V100 as above.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is exploratory. The aim is to reduce p95 for short-token requests without destabilizing throughput. Keep an eye on memory footprint of staging (tradeoff between B and ring size).
- Suggested review focus: correctness of buffer handshake and potential races, coherence with existing KV eviction (evict should not free an in-use staging buffer), and telemetry coverage.

References / context:
- Related tickets: JIRA-ENG-987 (paged-KV hot/cold experiments), CONFLUENCE-ENG-2345 (prefetch strategy doc), github PR referenced above.
- Slack thread: #serving-runtime "warp-bank streamer" (internal notes and early profiling graphs attached there)

TODO:
- [ ] Add unit test for buffer switch racing (simulate delayed stream)
- [ ] Add autotuner to pick coalescing window per deployment profile
- [ ] Validate with full model inference pipeline (not synthetic) and run load tests on dedicated cluster

End of note.
